title: Down the Well to the Meadow
text:
Once there were two people who had married, and each of them had a daughter of her own. The wife’s daughter was lazy and sluggish and never wanted to do a hand’s turn, but the man’s daughter was clever and willing; yet she could never satisfy her stepmother, and both the old wife and her daughter would gladly have been rid of her.

So one day they were to sit by the well and spin, both of them. The wife’s daughter was to spin flax, but the man’s daughter got nothing but stiff bristles. “You’re always so quick and handy, you are,” said the wife’s daughter, “but I’m not afraid to spin a match against you.” So they agreed that whichever one’s thread first snapped would have to go down into the well.

And before long it was the man’s daughter’s thread that broke, and down into the well she had to go. But when she reached the bottom she didn’t hurt herself, and far and wide she saw nothing but a lovely green meadow.

She walked a little way across the meadow, and came to a brushwood fence she had to cross. “Oh, don’t tread hard on me,” said the fence, “and I’ll help you another time.” So she made herself as light as a feather and stepped so gently and carefully that she scarcely touched it at all.

She went on a little farther and met a brindled cow with a milk-pail hanging from its horns. It was a big, fine cow, and its udder was so full and round. “Oh, please milk me,” said the cow, “for I’m so swollen with milk; drink as much as you like, and pour the rest over my hooves, and I’ll help you again.” The man’s daughter did as the cow asked: the moment she took hold of the teats the milk sprayed into the pail. She drank until her thirst was gone, poured what was left over the hooves, and hung the pail back on the cow’s horns.

After she had walked a bit more on the meadow, she met a great ram with wool so thick and long it dragged behind him, and from one horn hung a big pair of shears. “Oh, shear me,” said the ram, “for here I go with all this wool and panting, and it’s so hot I’m near to choking. Take as much as you want, and wind the rest around my neck, and I’ll help you again.” She was willing at once. The ram laid himself right in her lap and lay so still while she sheared him so neatly that she didn’t even scratch his skin. Then she took as much wool as she wanted and wound the rest around the ram’s neck.

A little farther on she came to an apple tree, so laden with apples that all its branches were bent down toward the ground, and beside the trunk stood a little pole. “Oh, please pick my apples,” said the tree, “so my branches can straighten up, for it’s a sore strain to stand so crooked; but do be gentle, so you don’t spoil me. Eat as much as you like, and lay the rest down by my roots, and I’ll help you again.” She picked the ones she could reach, and then took the pole and knocked down the others carefully. She ate her fill, and laid the rest neatly at the roots.

Then she walked a long, long way, until she came to a big farm where a troll-wife lived with her daughter. The girl went in and asked if she might have a place in service. “Oh, it’s no use,” said the troll-wife. “We’ve had many, but not one of them was good for anything.” But the girl pleaded so nicely that at last they took her in, and the troll-wife gave her a sieve and told her to fetch water in it.

She thought it was a foolish thing to carry water in a sieve, but she went all the same, and when she reached the well the little birds sang:

“Daub with clay,
plug with straw!
Daub with clay,
plug with straw!”

So she did, and then she could carry water in the sieve well enough. But when she came home with it and the troll-wife saw the sieve, she said, “You didn’t suck that out of your own breast!”

Then the troll-wife told her to go to the byre and muck out and milk the cows. But when she got there, there was a shovel so big and heavy she couldn’t manage it—couldn’t even lift it. She didn’t know what to do; but the birds sang she should take the handle of the broom and toss out a little, and all the rest would fly after it. She did so, and before you could blink the byre was as clean as if it had been both mucked and swept.

Next she was to milk the cows, but they were so restless—kicking and lashing out—that she couldn’t get near them. Then the birds outside sang:

“A little струй,
a little sup,
to all small birds—squirt it up!”

So she squirted a little stream of milk out to the small birds, and at once all the cows stood still and let her milk them; they didn’t kick or lash out, they never so much as lifted a hoof.

When the troll-wife saw her come in with the milk, she said again, “You didn’t suck that out of your own breast!

“But now you can take this black wool and wash it white.”

The girl had no idea how she was ever to finish such a task, for she had never seen anyone wash black wool white; still she said nothing, but took the wool and went out to the well with it. Then the little birds sang she should put the wool into the big tub standing there, and it would turn white enough. She did as they said.
imagePrompt: The Man’s Daughter, a clever, hardworking stepdaughter with a gentle expression, lands unharmed at the bottom of a deep well and rises to her feet in a lovely green meadow. She looks around in wonder at the bright grass and wildflowers spreading far and wide, the dark stone well-mouth behind her like a doorway from the world above, as soft sunlight washes the meadow in calm, storybook light.

title: The Blue Chest Chosen
text:
“No, no!” said the troll-wife when she came in with the wool. “There’s no use having you—you can do anything. In the end you’ll worry the life out of me. It’s best you get a travel pass.”

So the troll-wife set out three chests: one red, one green, and one blue. The girl might choose whichever she wanted as her wages. She didn’t know which to take, but the little birds sang:

“Take not the green,
take not the red;
but take the blue
that we have marked
with three crosses on top!”

So she took the blue one, just as the birds sang. “Shame on you, hill and dale!” said the troll-wife. “You’ll pay for that yet.”

When the man’s daughter was leaving, the troll-wife hurled a glowing iron bar after her. But the girl sprang behind the door at the same instant and hid, so it didn’t hit her—for the little birds had told her what to do.

Then she ran as fast as she could. But when she came to the apple tree she heard a deep rumbling along the road; it was the troll-wife and her daughter chasing after her. The girl was so frightened she didn’t know where to turn.

“Come here to me,” said the apple tree, “and I’ll help you. Go under my branches and hide, for if they catch you they’ll take the chest from you and tear you to pieces.” So she did. And soon enough the troll-wife and her daughter came.

“Have you seen a girl pass this way?” said the troll-wife.

“Oh yes,” said the apple tree, “one ran past here a little while ago; but she’s so far away now you’ll never catch her.”

So the troll-wife turned back and went home.

The girl went on a bit farther; but when she reached the ram, she heard that rumbling again, so loud she didn’t know where to put herself, so terrified was she—for she could well believe the troll-wife had changed her mind again.

“Come here to me and I’ll help you,” said the ram. “Hide under my wool and they won’t see you; otherwise they’ll take the chest and tear you to pieces.” At once she slipped beneath the wool, and before long the troll-wife came rushing up.

“Have you seen a girl pass this way?” she asked the ram.

“Oh yes,” said the ram, “I saw one a little while ago, but she ran so fast you won’t catch her.”

So the troll-wife turned and went home again.

When the girl had come as far as the cow, she heard the road rumble once more.

“Come here to me,” said the cow. “I’ll help you. Hide under my udder; otherwise the troll-wife will come and take your chest and tear you to pieces.” She hid there, and it wasn’t long before the troll-wife arrived.

“Have you seen a girl pass this way?” said the troll-wife to the cow.
imagePrompt: Inside the Troll-Wife’s remote farmhouse, The Troll-Wife—a harsh mistress—stands rigidly beside three chests set in a row: one red, one green, and one blue marked with three crosses on top. The Man’s Daughter reaches out and firmly takes the blue chest as her wages, while small Singing Birds hover nearby as if guiding her choice, and the troll-wife’s face tightens with anger at the selection.

title: Treasure in the Pigsty
text:
“Yes, I saw one a little while ago,” said the cow, “but she’s far off now, for she ran so fast. You won’t catch her.” And the troll-wife turned around and went home again.

The girl ran a long, long way, and when she was not far from the brushwood fence she heard that rumbling yet again, and she grew both frightened and sick at heart, for she knew the troll-wife had turned back once more.

“Come here to me and I’ll help you,” said the fence. “Creep under my twigs so they won’t see you; otherwise they’ll take the chest and tear you to pieces.” She hurried in under the twigs of the brushwood fence.

“Have you seen a girl pass this way?” asked the troll-wife.

“No, I haven’t seen any girl,” answered the fence, and it was so angry it hissed and spat, and swelled itself up so huge there was no thinking of getting over it. There was nothing for the troll-wife but to turn around and go home.

When the man’s daughter came safely home, the old wife and her daughter grew even more envious of her than before, for now she was even prettier, and so fine and shining it was a joy to look at her. They wouldn’t let her stay in the house with them; they drove her out to the pigsty, and there she had to live.

There she washed and scrubbed until it was neat and clean, and then she opened the chest to see what she had been paid. The moment she lifted the lid there was such a heap of gold and silver and such lovely things inside that both walls and roof were hung with it, and the pigsty was finer than the grandest king’s hall.

When her stepmother and stepsister saw this, they were beside themselves and began to ask what the service had been like. “Oh,” said the girl, “you can well imagine, since I got such wages. Such people, and such a mistress to serve, you’ll never find the like of.”

So at last the wife’s daughter was determined to go into service too, so she could get herself such a golden chest. They sat down to spin again; but this time the wife’s daughter was to spin bristles and the man’s daughter flax, and whoever’s thread snapped first was to go down into the well. It wasn’t long before the wife’s daughter’s thread broke—of course it did—and so they threw her into the well.

Everything went the same at first: she fell to the bottom without hurting herself and came to a beautiful green meadow. After she had gone a little way she came to the brushwood fence.

“Don’t tread hard on me, and I’ll help you again,” said the fence.

“Oh, what do I care about a heap of twigs!” she said, making herself heavy and stamping on the fence until it cracked and groaned.

Before long she came to the cow, swollen with milk.

“Please milk me,” said the cow, “and I’ll help you again; drink as much as you like, but pour the rest over my hooves.”

Yes, she milked the cow and drank as long as she could, but then there wasn’t a drop left to splash on the hooves. She flung the pail away over the hill and walked on.

After she had gone a bit more she came to the ram dragging his wool.

“Oh, please shear me, and I’ll serve you again,” said the ram. “Take as much wool as you like, but wind the rest around my neck.”

She did it, but so carelessly that she snipped great holes into his skin, and she took all the wool for herself.
imagePrompt: In a scrubbed, tidy pigsty turned radiant, The Man’s Daughter lifts the lid of the blue chest and a dazzling heap of gold, silver, and lovely things spills upward in glittering abundance. The humble wooden walls and roof seem hung with shining riches, transforming the pigsty into something finer than a king’s hall, while her gentle, astonished smile reflects the warm glow of her reward.

title: The Red Chest’s Curse
text:
A little while later she came to the apple tree, bent and crooked under its apples.

“Please pick my apples so my branches can straighten up, for it’s such a strain to stand so crooked,” said the apple tree. “But be careful so you don’t spoil me; eat as much as you like, but lay the rest neatly at my roots, and I’ll help you again.”

She picked what was closest and knocked down what she couldn’t reach with the pole, but she didn’t care a bit. She tore and beat down great branches, ate until she couldn’t swallow another bite, and then threw the rest under the tree.

When she had walked a little farther she came to the farm where the troll-wife lived, and begged for a place in service. The troll-wife said she didn’t want any maidservant, for either they were good for nothing or else they were too clever and cheated her out of what she had. But the wife’s daughter wouldn’t give in; she said she would have a place, and the troll-wife told her she might stay—if she was good for anything.

The first thing she had to do was fetch water in a sieve. So she went to the well and poured water into the sieve; but as fast as she poured it in, it ran right out again. Then the birds sang:

“Daub with clay,
plug with straw!
Daub with clay,
plug with straw!”

But she paid no attention to their singing; she threw clods of clay at the birds so they flew far away, and she had to go home again with an empty sieve, and got a thrashing from the troll-wife.

Then she was to muck out the byre and milk the cows; but she thought she was far too fine for such work. Still, she went into the byre; and there was the shovel, so big she couldn’t manage it at all. The birds told her the same as they had told the man’s daughter: take the broom-handle and toss out a little, and the rest would fly after. But she took the broom-handle and threw it at the birds.

When she tried to milk, the cows were so wild they kicked and lashed out, and every time she got a little in the pail they knocked it over. The birds sang:

“A little струй,
a little sup
to all small birds—squirt it up!”

But she beat and struck the cows, and flung and hurled whatever she could grab after the birds, and behaved like a mad thing. And she neither mucked nor milked anything. When she came in, the troll-wife both scolded her and beat her. And then she was to wash the black wool white, but that went no better.

This the troll-wife thought was too much, so she set out three chests—one red, one green, and one blue—and said she had no use for her, since she was good for nothing. Still, for wages she might choose whichever chest she wanted. Then the birds sang:

“Take not the green,
take not the red;
but take the blue
that we have marked
with three crosses on top!”

She didn’t care what the birds sang, but took the red one, since it glittered the most.

Then she set off for home, and she walked in perfect peace; no one chased after her. When she arrived, her mother was overjoyed, and at once they went into the great room and set the chest there, for they thought it held nothing but gold and silver, and imagined both walls and roof would be gilded. But when they opened it, out poured nothing but worms and toads. And whenever the wife’s daughter opened her mouth, it was the same: out came worms and toads and every crawling horror you can think of, until at last it was unbearable to be in the same house with her.

That was the wages she got for serving the troll-wife.
imagePrompt: In the great room at home, The Wife’s Daughter—lazy and selfish—throws open the red chest with eager hands, but instead of treasure, a revolting flood of worms and toads pours out onto the floor in writhing heaps. Her face twists from triumph to horror as the crawling horrors spread, the room’s hopeful atmosphere collapsing into disgust and dread.
